beginner: Sweet potatoes want loose, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil that the swelling storage roots can push through easily. Light soil on raised ridges or mounds is ideal, because it drains well and gives the roots room to grow smooth and long. Heavy, wet clay is the thing to avoid: it stays soggy, rots the roots, and forces them into short, knobby shapes. If your soil is heavy, build up a ridge or a raised bed of loose mix, which also warms up faster in spring. Keep the soil slightly acidic, about pH 5.8 to 6.5. Go easy on nitrogen and fresh manure, which grow lots of leafy vine and few roots.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes yield best in loose, friable, well-drained sandy loam worked into raised ridges or mounds, which give the developing storage roots room to expand and keep them out of standing water. A light, warm soil produces the longest, smoothest roots; cold, heavy, poorly drained clay stays wet, rots roots, and produces short and misshapen ones, and is best improved with organic matter or replaced with a built-up ridge or raised bed. Hold the soil slightly acidic, roughly pH 5.8 to 6.5. Keep nitrogen modest and avoid fresh manure: rich, high-nitrogen ground drives rampant vine growth at the expense of roots. Even, moderate moisture in free-draining soil is the goal, never waterlogged ground.

beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Sweet potatoes like it slightly acidic, about 5.8 to 6.5, which is close to what most vegetables want. They are not fussy and will grow from about 5.0 up to nearly neutral, so you rarely need to change your soil much. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number, and if your soil is very alkaline, mixing in compost helps. Do not overdo lime.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes grow best in slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 5.8 to 6.5 (University of Georgia gives 6.0 to 6.5). They are adaptable and will crop from about 5.0 up toward neutral, so pH is rarely the limiting factor. Where soil pox and Streptomyces soil rot are a problem on susceptible varieties, growers avoid pushing the pH high and lean on resistant cultivars rather than heavy liming. Amend very alkaline ground with organic matter and confirm your starting point with a soil test before planting.

beginner: Sweet potatoes do not need much feeding, and too much of the wrong kind backfires. Mix a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 into the ridge before you plant, then feed once more about a month after setting the slips. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer or fresh manure: that grows a jungle of leafy vine and hardly any sweet potatoes underneath. A little compost worked into the bed is the safe way to enrich it.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are light feeders and specifically want restrained nitrogen. University of Georgia suggests working in about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet before planting, then side-dressing roughly 4 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row about 4 to 6 weeks after transplanting. Favor a low-nitrogen, higher-potassium ratio: too much nitrogen (and fresh manure) grows lush, sprawling vine and few storage roots, while adequate potassium supports root sizing and quality.

beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Sweet potatoes do best with a low first number, like 5-10-10, not a high-nitrogen feed. Too much nitrogen grows leaves and vines instead of sweet potatoes, so use a low-nitrogen fertilizer and some compost.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are light feeders that want low nitrogen and good potassium. A blend such as 5-10-10 worked into the ridge before planting covers most home soils. Excess nitrogen drives vine at the expense of roots, and fresh manure has the same effect, so lean on a low-nitrogen fertilizer and compost rather than a balanced or high-nitrogen feed.

beginner: Mix in about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet before planting, then side-dress lightly about a month later. Go easy: more fertilizer, especially nitrogen, grows more leaves, not more sweet potatoes.
seasoned: Work about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet into the ridge before planting (UGA), then side-dress about 4 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row roughly 4 to 6 weeks after transplanting. Keep nitrogen low; excess nitrogen grows vine at the expense of storage roots.

beginner: Sweet potatoes are easygoing and take up a lot of ground with their sprawling vines, so companions are mostly about using the edges of the bed. Bush beans and other legumes are a sensible neighbor because they add nitrogen to the soil. The main thing to avoid is crowding them next to other sprawling vine crops like squash and pumpkins, which fight for the same space and sunlight. Do not trust every companion chart online; many of their claims have never been tested.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are undemanding neighbors but greedy for space, since a single plant can run vines many feet in every direction. The best-grounded pairing is with legumes (bush beans, southern peas), which fix nitrogen and share the bed without heavy competition. Aromatic herbs are a traditional edge planting. The clearest practical avoids are other rampant vine crops, squash, pumpkins, and melons, which compete for the same ground and light. Most companion-chart claims for sweet potato are folklore; treat them with healthy skepticism, since university reviews find little evidence behind most of them.

beginner: Beans are legumes that pull nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil, which suits sweet potatoes since they want only modest nitrogen. Bush beans stay compact and can share the edge of the bed without fighting the vines for space.
seasoned: Bush beans and other legumes are a sensible sweet potato neighbor: they fix nitrogen and, being compact and upright, do not compete hard with the ground-running vines. The nitrogen contribution is a real mechanism; treat the pairing as a grounded tradition rather than a measured yield effect.

beginner: Some gardeners plant strong-smelling herbs around the edge of the sweet potato patch in the hope of confusing pests. It is a traditional idea rather than a proven one, but the herbs use the border space the vines do not need early on.
seasoned: Aromatic herbs at the border are a traditional pest-confusion planting with no controlled evidence behind it for sweet potato. Recorded as hedged tradition; the concrete value is filling edge space the vines reach only later in the season.

beginner: These are all big, sprawling vine crops, just like sweet potatoes. Grown side by side they smother each other and fight for the same sunlight and ground, so give each its own space in the garden.
seasoned: Cucurbits (squash, pumpkins, melons) are rampant ground-running vines like sweet potato, so interplanting them means two sprawling crops competing for the same ground and light. This is a habit-based space conflict, not a shared-disease risk, and the fix is simply separate beds.

beginner: Small holes and dark, spongy tunnels inside the sweet potatoes, which you usually find only when you dig or slice them. Even a little feeding makes the roots taste bitter and smell off, so they are no longer good to eat. The beetle itself is a slim, ant-like weevil with a long snout, reddish legs, and a shiny blue-black body. It is the worst sweet potato pest, especially in the Deep South.
seasoned: Small holes and dark, spongy tunnels running through the storage roots, found when you dig or cut them. Even light feeding triggers a chemical reaction that gives the roots a bitter taste and an off, turpentine-like odor, ruining them for eating. The adult is a slender, ant-like weevil, about a quarter inch long, with a dark head and snout, reddish legs, and a metallic blue-black body; you may see chewing on stems and leaves. This is the single most serious pest of sweet potato, worst in the Deep South and Gulf.

beginner: A small weevil called the sweet potato weevil. Its grubs tunnel through the sweet potatoes and stems, and the plant reacts by turning bitter, so even lightly damaged roots are ruined. It rides in on infested slips and survives in leftover sweet potatoes in the ground, and it keeps damaging the crop even after harvest in storage.
seasoned: The sweet potato weevil (Cylas formicarius, family Brentidae). Larvae do the principal damage by mining tunnels through the storage roots (and stems), leaving them riddled with cavities, spongy, and darkened; the feeding induces bitter terpenes even at low levels. It breeds continuously in warm climates, spreads mainly on infested slips and in leftover roots, and continues to damage the crop in storage.

beginner: You cannot fix sweet potatoes that are already tunneled, so throw them out. The whole game is prevention: plant only certified weevil-free slips, and clean up every leftover or volunteer sweet potato in the ground after harvest, because the weevil lives on in them. Dig your crop on time instead of leaving it in the soil, and do not plant next to last year's bed.
seasoned: There is no rescue for tunneled roots; discard them. Control is prevention: start only with certified weevil-free slips, and practice strict sanitation, removing and destroying every leftover, cull, and volunteer root that can harbor the weevil between crops. Harvest promptly once the crop matures rather than leaving roots in infested soil, and keep new plantings away from last year's beds and from stored roots.

beginner: Start with certified weevil-free slips, not saved sweet potatoes. Move the patch to a new spot each year, well away from where sweet potatoes grew before and away from where you store them. After you dig, clean up every leftover and volunteer root, because the weevil survives in them. Harvest on time rather than leaving the crop in the ground.
seasoned: Buy certified, weevil-free slips rather than saving your own or using field-run roots. Rotate sweet potatoes well away from last year's beds and from any sweet potato storage, since the weevil moves only short distances. Remove all volunteer and cull roots after harvest, harvest promptly, and in badly infested areas grow on a strict rotation with a fallow break. Certified slips plus sanitation carry nearly all of the control.

beginner: Narrow holes and shallow tracks drilled into the sweet potatoes, found when you dig them. They are made by hard, shiny soil worms (wireworms) and the grubs of cucumber and flea beetles. You do not see anything above ground; you find the little tunnels and pits at harvest, and damaged roots do not store as well.
seasoned: Narrow holes and shallow, winding grooves bored straight into the storage roots, leaving pinhole punctures and tracks that downgrade quality and open the door to storage rots. The culprits are slender, shiny, hard-bodied wireworms (click beetle larvae) plus the larvae of cucumber beetles and flea beetles (the wireworm, Diabrotica, Systena complex). There are no useful aboveground signs; the damage is found at harvest.

beginner: Wireworms are the larvae of click beetles; they live in the soil for years and are worst in beds that were lawn, grass, or corn not long ago. The larvae of cucumber beetles and flea beetles do similar damage, moving into the soil to nibble the sweet potatoes as they grow.
seasoned: Wireworms are click beetle larvae that live in the soil for several years and are most numerous in ground recently in sod, grass, or corn. The same root-scarring complex includes larvae of spotted and banded cucumber beetles (Diabrotica) and flea beetles (Systena), which move into the soil to feed on the developing roots through the season.

beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already tunneled, so cut out the bad spots and eat those first instead of storing them. Dig the crop on time rather than leaving it in the ground, where the worms keep boring, and keep grassy weeds down.
seasoned: There is no rescue for scarred roots; trim damaged areas and use those roots first rather than storing them. Harvest promptly once the crop matures rather than leaving roots in infested soil, where feeding accumulates. Keeping the ground worked and free of grassy weeds reduces the habitat these larvae favor.

beginner: Do not plant sweet potatoes in a bed that was grass, lawn, or corn in the last year or two, where wireworms are worst. Rotate your crops, work the soil, pull grassy weeds, and dig on time. If wireworms keep ruining a bed, use a raised bed with clean soil.
seasoned: Avoid planting sweet potatoes in ground that was recently pasture, lawn, or corn, where wireworm numbers peak; extend the interval between grass and a root crop. Rotate, keep the soil well worked, control grassy weeds, and harvest on time. Where wireworm history is bad, grow elsewhere or in clean raised-bed soil.

beginner: Lots of tiny holes in the leaves, as if peppered with shot, made by little dark beetles that hop away when you come near. Young slips are hurt most; big, healthy vines shrug it off. The grubs in the soil can also scar the sweet potatoes.
seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed and chew many small round shot-holes in the leaves. Heavy early feeding on young transplants stunts growth; the soil-dwelling larvae also scar the developing storage roots. Established, vigorously running plants usually outgrow light foliage feeding.

beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that spend winter nearby and jump onto young sweet potato plants. They do the most harm to freshly set slips and in warm, dry spells, and their grubs can scar the roots underground.
seasoned: Several species of small flea beetles that overwinter nearby and move onto young sweet potato foliage in spring and early summer. They are worst on small, slow transplants and in warm, dry weather; their larvae contribute to the root-scarring complex below ground.

beginner: Keep young slips growing strong with steady water and they usually outgrow the damage as the vines take off. A row cover protects them early on, and clearing weeds and old plant debris takes away their winter hiding spots.
seasoned: Healthy, well-watered transplants usually outgrow flea beetle feeding once the vines run. Floating row cover protects young plants during the vulnerable first weeks; remove it as the vines begin to sprawl. Clearing weeds and old crop debris reduces the shelter they overwinter in.

beginner: Move the patch to a new spot, pull weeds, and cover the young slips until they are established and the vines start to run. Plants that are well watered handle flea beetles much better than struggling ones.
seasoned: Rotate away from last year's beds, keep the area weed-free, and protect freshly set slips with row cover until they are established and running. Vigorous, evenly watered transplants tolerate feeding far better than stressed ones.

beginner: Tiny white flying insects that scatter in a cloud when you brush the leaves, clustered underneath with a sticky film. Their feeding is minor, but they can pass on plant viruses that mottle and curl the leaves and cut your harvest. A plant that catches a virus will not get better.
seasoned: Clouds of tiny white, moth-like insects that lift off the foliage when disturbed, clustered on leaf undersides with sticky honeydew and sooty mold. The bigger problem is not their feeding but the viruses they transmit (such as sweet potato feathery mottle virus and sweet potato leaf curl virus), which mottle, curl, and stunt the foliage and erode yield over time; virus-infected plants do not recover.

beginner: Whiteflies are tiny sap-sucking insects, and as they move from plant to plant they carry sweet potato viruses. The viruses, more than the bugs, are the real concern, which is why it is best to plant certified, disease-tested slips instead of saving your own.
seasoned: Whiteflies colonize sweet potato foliage and, as they move plant to plant, transmit sweet potato viruses. Virus pressure, not the feeding itself, is the main reason to manage them, and it is the reason growers are advised to start from certified, virus-tested slips rather than saved or field-run material.

beginner: Plant certified, disease-tested slips so the patch starts clean. A few whiteflies are fine, because helpful bugs usually keep them in check; for heavy clusters, spray them off with water or use insecticidal soap. Pull and throw away any plant that clearly has a virus.
seasoned: Start with certified, virus-tested slips to keep virus out of the patch. Tolerate light whitefly numbers, since beneficial insects often control them; a strong spray of water or insecticidal soap knocks down heavy colonies on the leaf undersides. Remove and destroy any plant showing clear virus symptoms.

beginner: Buy certified slips, avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful bugs, keep weeds down, and pull out any virus-looking plant right away. Do not save slips from a patch that had virus, because it comes back with them.
seasoned: Use certified slips, encourage beneficial insects by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, control nearby weeds that host whiteflies and virus, and rogue out virus-symptomatic plants promptly. Do not save and replant slips from a patch that showed virus, since it carries over.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant, and the vine is stunted; if you slit a stem near the base you see brown streaks inside. Badly affected plants wilt and die before making sweet potatoes. It usually comes in on infected slips or from the soil.
seasoned: Yellowing and wilting that starts on the lower leaves and progresses up the vine, often on one side, with stunting; a lengthwise cut of the stem near the base shows a brown, discolored streak in the water-conducting tissue. Plants may collapse before making a crop. It moves up from infected slips or through the soil.

beginner: A soil fungus (Fusarium oxysporum) that gets into the roots and stem and clogs the plant's plumbing. It lives in the soil for years and rides in on infected slips, and it builds up if you grow sweet potatoes in the same spot again and again.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum, which enters through the roots and stem base and plugs the vascular tissue. It survives for years in the soil and is carried on infected slips, so it builds up where sweet potatoes are grown repeatedly in the same ground.

beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant, so pull it and throw it away (do not compost it). There is no spray fix; you prevent it with clean slips, resistant varieties, and rotating the bed.
seasoned: There is no cure for an infected plant; remove and destroy it. Management is preventive and variety-based: it is controlled by clean slips, resistant cultivars, and rotation, not by a spray.

beginner: Plant certified, disease-free slips and choose a wilt-resistant variety if this has been a problem. Do not grow sweet potatoes in the same bed year after year, and never save slips from a patch that wilted.
seasoned: Start with certified, disease-free slips and grow Fusarium-resistant varieties (such as Sumor or other wilt-resistant releases) where the disease occurs. Rotate sweet potatoes out of an infected bed for several years, and do not save slips from a patch that showed wilt.

beginner: Plants that are stunted and wilt easily even with water, and sweet potatoes that come up cracked, bumpy, and rough-skinned with little knots on them. The damage is worst in sandy soil and hot regions. You usually see it clearly only when you dig the roots.
seasoned: Stunted, off-color, wilt-prone vines above ground, and below ground storage roots that are cracked, bumpy, and galled, with small knots and rough, split skin that downgrade quality and storage. The southern root-knot nematode is the main species, and damage is worst in sandy soils and warm regions.

beginner: A microscopic soil roundworm (the southern root-knot nematode) that attacks the roots and makes them crack and knot. It lives in the soil and feeds on many crops, so it builds up when you grow the same kinds of plants in one spot over and over.
seasoned: The southern root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita), a microscopic soil roundworm that invades the roots, causing galling and the cracked, bumpy roots that grade out. It persists in the soil and on many hosts, so it builds up where susceptible crops are grown repeatedly.

beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already cracked and knotted. Instead, prevent it: grow a nematode-resistant variety, rotate the bed to different crops, and build up the soil with compost. In hot climates, covering moist soil with clear plastic through the summer can knock the numbers down.
seasoned: There is no rescue for galled, cracked roots. Management is preventive: grow nematode-resistant varieties, rotate to non-host or less-susceptible crops, and keep the soil high in organic matter. Solarizing the bed in the hot months and cover cropping can lower populations over time.

beginner: Grow a nematode-resistant variety like Centennial or Covington, rotate your crops so sweet potatoes and their susceptible cousins are not in the same bed each year, and add plenty of compost. Start with certified, clean slips.
seasoned: Choose root-knot-resistant varieties (such as Centennial, Covington, or other resistant releases), rotate away from susceptible hosts on a multi-year cycle, and raise soil organic matter. Start with certified, clean slips so you do not introduce new populations.

beginner: Dark, sunken, round spots on the sweet potatoes, firm and greenish-black to brown, and the affected part can taste bitter. It also shows as dark patches on the lower stems. It gets worse in storage and comes in on infected slips or from the soil.
seasoned: Round, dark, sunken lesions on the storage roots that are firm and greenish-black to dark brown, sometimes with a bitter taste in the affected tissue; on the lower stems it shows as dark cankers. It spreads in storage and in the field from infected slips and contaminated soil, and it is a major cause of cull and storage loss.

beginner: A fungus (Ceratocystis fimbriata) that gets into the roots and stems through cuts and bruises, lives in the soil and on old plant debris, and rides in on infected slips. It likes warm, damp conditions and keeps spreading on stored sweet potatoes.
seasoned: The fungus Ceratocystis fimbriata, which infects roots and stems through wounds, survives in soil and crop debris, and is spread on infected slips and by handling. Warmth and moisture favor it, and it continues to develop on stored roots.

beginner: You cannot cure an infected sweet potato, so throw out affected ones and never store damaged roots. The fix is prevention: clean slips, gentle handling, curing right after harvest, and keeping tools and bins clean.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected roots; discard them and do not store blemished ones. Management is preventive: clean slips, careful handling to avoid wounds, prompt curing, and sanitation.

beginner: Use certified, disease-free slips, rotate the bed, and handle the sweet potatoes gently so you do not bruise them, since the fungus enters through cuts. Cure the crop right after digging and clean up leftover roots.
seasoned: Start with certified, disease-free slips from clean stock, rotate out of infected beds, handle roots gently to avoid the wounds the fungus enters through, and cure the crop promptly after harvest. Discard cull and volunteer roots that carry the fungus over.

beginner: Scurf is dark brown to black blotches on the skin of the sweet potato; it does not rot the inside, but it makes the roots look poor and dry out faster in storage. Soft rot turns bruised or too-cold roots into a soft, wet, smelly mush in the bin. Both are worst on damaged roots that were not cured or were stored wrong.
seasoned: Scurf shows as brown to blackish blotches on the skin surface that do not penetrate the flesh; it is a cosmetic, skin-quality problem that also increases moisture loss and shrinkage in storage. Bacterial and fungal soft rots turn wounded or chilled roots into a soft, wet, sometimes foul mush in storage. Both are worst on bruised, poorly cured, or improperly stored roots.

beginner: Scurf is a skin fungus that comes in on infected slips and lives in the soil. Soft rot is caused by bacteria and fungi that get into bruised roots, especially when the sweet potatoes were not cured or were stored too cold or too wet.
seasoned: Scurf is caused by the fungus Monilochaetes infuscans, carried on infected slips and in soil, and confined to the skin. Storage soft rots are caused by bacteria and fungi (including Rhizopus) that enter through wounds and are favored by bruising, poor curing, and cold or damp storage.

beginner: You cannot fix scurf or soft rot. Scurfy sweet potatoes are still fine to eat once peeled, but soft, rotting ones should be thrown out. Prevent both with clean slips, gentle handling, curing, and proper warm storage.
seasoned: There is no rescue for scurfed or rotting roots; scurfed ones are safe to eat after peeling, but soft-rotted ones are discarded. Management is preventive: clean slips, careful handling, prompt curing, and correct warm storage.

beginner: Plant certified, clean slips, rotate the bed, and be gentle with the sweet potatoes so you do not bruise them. Cure them warm and humid right after digging so the skins heal, then store them warm (not in the fridge), and never store damaged roots.
seasoned: Use certified, scurf-free slips, rotate out of infected beds, and handle roots gently to avoid wounds. Cure the crop warm and humid right after harvest to heal skins, then store warm (never cold or wet), and do not store bruised or diseased roots.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly, moderately damp, especially right after planting the slips and later while the sweet potatoes are sizing up. Give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings. Once the vines are growing well the plants handle dry spells fairly well, but letting the soil go dry and then soaking it while the roots form makes them crack. Cut back on water in the last few weeks before you dig.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes want even, moderate moisture, especially while the slips establish and again while the storage roots are sizing. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings. Once well established the deep root system makes them fairly drought tolerant, but a prolonged dry-then-wet swing during root bulking causes cracked and misshapen roots. Ease off water in the last few weeks before harvest so the roots do not split and the skins firm up.

beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, and a bit more in hot or sandy conditions. Water most attentively right after planting and while the roots are sizing. Ease off in the last couple of weeks before harvest so the sweet potatoes do not split.
seasoned: About 1 inch per week including rainfall, more in heat or sandy soil, concentrated at establishment and during root bulking. Do not keep the ridge waterlogged. Taper off in the last 2 to 3 weeks before harvest to reduce cracking and let the skins set.

beginner: Water at the soil, keeping the ridge damp but not soggy. A layer of mulch early on helps hold steady moisture and keep weeds down until the vines spread out and shade the ground themselves.
seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line where practical, and keep the raised ridge moist but never waterlogged. A mulch helps hold even moisture and smother weeds while the vines fill in, though the sprawling canopy soon shades the ground itself.

beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, the sweet potatoes rot. Watch for yellowing, wilting even though the soil is wet, a sour-smelling soggy bed, and soft or split roots; if you see these, water less and fix the drainage.
seasoned: Constantly saturated soil rots the roots and drives soft rot and black rot; yellowing, wilting despite wet soil, a sour waterlogged ridge, and soft or cracked roots are signs to back off and improve drainage. Waterlogging is worse than short drought for this crop.

beginner: Droopy leaves in the afternoon, dull color, and slow growth mean the plants are thirsty, which matters most just after planting and while the roots size up. The bigger problem is letting the soil go dry and then flooding it, which cracks the sweet potatoes.
seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day, dull, small foliage, and slow vine growth signal too little water, most critical during establishment and root sizing. The sharper risk is an irregular dry-then-soaked cycle during bulking, which cracks and misshapes the roots.

beginner: Right after planting the slips, keep the ridge evenly damp for the first couple of weeks while they root in. This is a key time. Keep it moist but never soggy, since waterlogging is worse for sweet potatoes than a dry spell.
seasoned: The first make-or-break window: keep the ridge evenly, moderately moist for the 2 to 3 weeks while the slips root in. Water at the base and never let the ridge stay waterlogged, which this crop resents more than short drought.

beginner: As the vines spread, water about an inch a week, keeping the ridge damp but not soggy. A layer of mulch early on holds the moisture and keeps weeds down until the vines shade the ground.
seasoned: As the vines run, keep about an inch a week at the base, ridge moist but never waterlogged. Mulch early holds even moisture and smothers weeds until the sprawling canopy shades the ground itself.

beginner: As the sweet potatoes begin to form, keep the soil evenly moist. Steady, well-drained soil now sets how many roots the plant will grow.
seasoned: As storage roots begin to form, hold even moisture at the root zone; steady, well-drained conditions now set the number of roots the plant will size up.

beginner: While the sweet potatoes are sizing up, keep the water steady. Letting the soil go dry and then soaking it is what makes the roots crack and grow knobby, so even moisture is the key.
seasoned: The second make-or-break window: while the storage roots size up from about mid-season, even moisture sets their size and shape, and a prolonged dry-then-wet swing here is exactly what cracks and misshapes the roots. Keep it steady, more in heat or sandy soil, and never waterlog the ridge.

beginner: Cut back on water in the last couple of weeks before you dig. The dry finish keeps the sweet potatoes from splitting and firms up their skins so they store well.
seasoned: Ease off water in the last 2 to 3 weeks before digging so the roots do not split and the skins firm up for storage. A well-cured skin set in dry-finished soil stores far better.

beginner: Water the ridge evenly and never let it stay soggy. Grown-in sweet potatoes handle dry spells fairly well, but on-again off-again watering while the roots form makes them crack, so aim for even moisture and good drainage.
seasoned: Keep moisture even at the root zone and avoid waterlogging the ridge. Established sweet potatoes tolerate some drought, but uneven soil moisture during root formation drives cracked and knobby roots, so steady base watering plus a well-drained ridge is the goal.

beginner: The most important times to keep the soil evenly moist are the first couple of weeks after planting the slips, and later while the sweet potatoes are sizing up. Then water less in the last few weeks before harvest so the roots firm up and do not crack.
seasoned: The two make-or-break windows are establishment (the first 2 to 3 weeks, while slips root in) and root bulking (from about mid-season on), when even moisture sets root number, size, and shape. Then ease watering in the final weeks so skins set and roots do not split for storage.

beginner: You grow sweet potatoes from slips, which are rooted sprouts, not from seedlings you started indoors, so there is not much to harden off. If your slips came from a greenhouse, set them in the shade for a day or two first. Plant them out only after all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F, and keep them watered for the first week or two. They often wilt at first and then perk up, which is normal.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are set out as slips (rooted sprouts), not seed-raised seedlings, so there is little to harden off. Field-pulled or bought slips are already acclimated; greenhouse-grown slips benefit from a day or two in shade before planting. Set slips out only once all frost danger has passed and the soil is reliably above about 65°F, and keep them well watered for the first week or two while they root in, since they often wilt at first and then recover.

beginner: Grow sweet potatoes from slips, which are rooted sprouts. You can buy them as certified disease-free plants, or grow your own by half-burying a healthy sweet potato in warm, damp soil about 6 weeks ahead and pulling off the sprouts once they have roots. Plant the slips 3 to 4 inches deep, with a couple of the leaf joints buried, spacing them 12 to 18 inches apart along ridges or mounds in rows about 3 to 4 feet apart. Wait until all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F. There is nothing to start from seed indoors. In cool-summer areas, laying down black plastic warms the soil and gives you extra time.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are grown from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root, not from seed and not from seed-potato-style pieces. Buy certified, disease-free and weevil-free slips, or bed a healthy root in warm, moist medium about 6 weeks ahead and pull the sprouts once they have roots. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep with two or more nodes buried, spacing them 12 to 18 inches apart on ridges or mounds in rows 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost danger has passed and the soil is above about 65°F (70 to 80°F is better). There is no indoor seed-starting step; the slip itself is the transplant. In short-season areas, planting through black plastic warms the soil and buys extra growing days.

beginner: Use a big, deep container so the sweet potatoes have room to form, and expect the vines to trail over the sides. beginner: Sweet potatoes are a warm-weather crop grown for the sweet, starchy roots that form underground. Despite the name, they are not related to regular potatoes; they belong to the morning glory family. You do not grow them from seed or from tubers. Instead you plant slips, which are rooted sprouts, set out only after all frost is past and the soil is warm. The plants send out long, trailing vines that cover the ground, so they are grown on ridges or mounds with plenty of room. Sweet potatoes need a long, hot summer (about 3 to 4 months of warm, frost-free weather) and they love heat, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the desert Southwest are the best places to grow them, while cooler northern gardens are a stretch and use black plastic and fast varieties. Go easy on fertilizer, especially nitrogen, or you get lots of vine and few sweet potatoes. Dig the crop before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cure the roots somewhere warm and humid for a week or two, which heals the skins and makes them sweet, and store them warm, around 55 to 60°F. Never put sweet potatoes in the fridge or anywhere cold, which ruins them. This is the opposite of how you store regular potatoes. The young leaves are also good to eat as a cooked green.
seasoned: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a warm-season, frost-tender member of the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae), not a nightshade and unrelated to the ordinary potato despite the shared name. It is grown for its swollen storage roots and planted not from seed or tubers but from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root and set out only after all frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, above about 65°F. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling groundcover, running long vines that root at the nodes, and it is grown on raised ridges or mounds that drain well and give the roots room to expand. The crop needs a long, hot season, roughly 90 to 120 frost-free days, and it relishes the summer heat that stalls many other vegetables, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the low deserts are its stronghold while short-season northern gardens are marginal and lean on black plastic and fast varieties. Feed sparingly and keep nitrogen low, since rich ground grows rampant vine and few roots. The crop is dug before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cured warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F at high humidity for one to two weeks) to heal the skins and turn starch to sugar, and stored warm, near 55 to 60°F. Sweet potatoes are damaged by cold and must never be refrigerated or stored below about 50 to 55°F, the opposite of white potato storage. The young leaves and shoots are also edible as a cooked green.

beginner: You harvest sweet potatoes by the calendar and, most importantly, before frost, not by watching the tops die back. They are usually ready about 3 to 4 months after planting, when the roots are full size; the older leaves may yellow, but unlike regular potatoes the vines do not obviously die down. Dig before the first fall frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots. Loosen the soil with a fork well away from the plant so you do not stab the sweet potatoes, lift them gently, and handle them carefully because they bruise easily and the skins are thin at first. Let them dry off out of the sun, do not wash them, then cure them somewhere warm and humid for a week or two before storing. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are harvested by days-to-maturity and, above all, before frost, not by a die-back signal. The crop is usually ready about 90 to 120 days from transplanting slips, when the roots have reached full size; the oldest leaves may yellow, but the vines do not clearly die back the way potato tops do. Dig before the first fall frost, since frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots and shortens storage. Loosen the soil with a fork well outside the plant so you do not spear or bruise the roots, lift them gently, and handle them carefully, since sweet potatoes bruise easily and skins are thin at harvest. Let them dry briefly out of direct sun, do not wash them, then cure warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F for one to two weeks, before storing. If a frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two so rot does not travel down into the roots.

beginner: Getting the soil right matters for sweet potatoes. Loosen the bed deep, mix in compost, and mound the soil up into ridges about 8 to 10 inches high, which drain well, warm up faster, and give the roots room to grow long and smooth. Heavy, cold, soggy clay rots the roots and makes them lumpy, so use ridges or a raised bed if your soil is clay. Keep the soil slightly acidic (pH about 5.8 to 6.5). Go easy on fertilizer and skip fresh manure, which grow leaves instead of roots; use a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 and a little compost. Plant the slips 3 to 4 inches deep and 12 to 18 inches apart along the ridge, in rows about 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F. In cooler areas, lay down black plastic to warm the soil and buy extra time.
seasoned: Sweet potato quality starts with loose, warm, well-drained soil built up into ridges or mounds. Work the bed deep, incorporate compost, and form ridges 8 to 10 inches high, which drain well, warm quickly, and give the storage roots room to expand smoothly; heavy clay stays cold and wet, rots roots, and forces short, knobby shapes, and is best improved with organic matter or grown in raised ridges. Aim for a slightly acidic pH, roughly 5.8 to 6.5. Keep nitrogen low and avoid fresh manure, which drive rampant vine at the expense of roots; use a low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 and modest compost. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep, 12 to 18 inches apart along the ridge in rows 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost is past and the soil is above about 65°F. In short-season areas, lay black plastic to warm the soil and add growing days.
